extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science; philosophers of science; scientists interested in scientific method and classification
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and methodological criteria for classifying the sciences and conducting scientific inquiry, emphasizing parsimony, empirical authentication, provisional classification, and caution in generalising laws across domains. Intended as prescriptive principles for how to reason about, describe, and organise scientific knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best form for classification (branching tree with interdependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: From Bacon we learn that the best form for classification is that of a branching tree, but from Comte that there is in reality an interdependence in the sciences, so that a clear understanding of one may necessitate a previous study of several others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a branching-tree model for classification where useful, but recognise and accommodate interdependencies between disciplines; avoid a rigid tree that ignores cross-links or prerequisite knowledge in related fields. Expect classifications to be provisional as sciences develop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental distinction: Abstract vs Concrete Science
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt Spencer's fundamental distinction between Abstract and Concrete Science, or those which deal respectively with the modes and the contents of perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or analysing sciences, separate concerns about modes (abstract/formal structures, e.g., mathematics) from contents (concrete, perceptual phenomena, e.g., physics, biology). This distinction guides how subjects are grouped and studied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three fundamental divisions and their links
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three fundamental divisions corresponding to Abstract, Physical, and Biological Sciences which are united pair and pair by Applied Mathematics and Bio-physics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Applied Mathematics and Biophysics as cross-linking disciplines that connect abstract theory to physical and biological phenomena. Pursue work in these linking fields to integrate understanding across divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of principles (Occam's Razor / parsimony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither more, nor more onerous, causes are to be assumed, than are necessary to account for the phenomena. (Occam: Entia non sunt multiplicanda pr®ter necessitatem.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parsimony as a canon of scientific thought within the sphere of perception: avoid multiplying entities or causes beyond what is necessary to explain observations. Do not extend the notion of 'simplicity' as a metaphysical dogma beyond empirical description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional nature of classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual even with great ability must fail for want of specialists' knowledge to classify the sciences satisfactorily. A group of scientists might achieve much more, but even their system would only have temporary value as the position of a science relative to others changes with its development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat any classification as temporary and revisable. Prefer collaborative, specialist-informed classifications and be ready to update systems as disciplines evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific descriptions are conceptual summaries, not teleological final causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural law is a product of the human reason and the correlated growth of reasoning and perceptive faculties; scientific mastery denotes description of perceptual routine in brief conceptual formulae, not transcendental exegesis of final causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame scientific statements as historically grounded summaries of perceptual experience. Avoid claiming metaphysical or teleological explanations beyond what observation and rational analysis support; where knowledge lacks, confess ignorance honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dare to be ignorant; remain agnostic until evidence suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: We must turn a deaf ear to all those who would suggest that we can enter the stronghold of truth by the burrow of superstition, or scale its walls by the ladder of metaphysics. We must dare to be ignorant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from adopting speculative causal hypotheses (superstition, metaphysics) in the absence of sufficient empirical support. Maintain agnosticism where no adequate perceptual formula exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for empirical evidence and authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of long-term biological facts (e.g., maximum period seeds retain vitality) is hampered by slow experiments and frequently weak provenance; combined evidence of ancient origin and actual germination often fails to reach the point of legal testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand well-documented provenance, reproducible experiments, and rigorous authentication for empirical claims—especially historical or exceptional claims. Treat anecdotal, poorly-documented, or single-observer reports with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in extending physical laws across scales or contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater caution is necessary than is sometimes observed in extending Newton's third law to molecules or atoms, which may have oscillatory motion relative to an intervening medium (ether) and so might not strictly obey the law in the simple form applied to gross matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid uncritical generalisation of laws derived for one scale/domain to others without examining intervening mechanisms (e.g., media, delays, non-colinearity). Recognise that a law may be an adequate description for 'gross matter' but require revision at micro scales or different physical regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret experimental results in the context of all known facts
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot say what would happen if the earth did not rotate; we must interpret the single experiment as it is presented to us and bring it into unison with other facts known to us and not with our arbitrary imaginings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place experimental observations within the broader body of empirical knowledge when drawing conclusions. Be wary of counterfactual overreach; test interpretations against other relevant facts and observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish perceptual and conceptual spheres; avoid category confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse perception (appreciation of sense-impressions) with conceptual constructs (the routine of perception or moving ideals). Confusion of the perceptual and the conceptual leads to illegitimate inferences (e.g., Wallace's conflation of matter, force, and will-force).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear separation between empirical observations and theoretical/conceptual models. Use terminology consistently to avoid drawing unwarranted conclusions by equivocation between levels of description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual constructs must be grounded in perceptual facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A line conceived as having no relative accelerations in its parts is defined as having a fixed direction in space; the statement that a path will be a straight line is the perceptual statement of the principle of inertia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that conceptual definitions and mathematical constructs correspond to perceptual or experimental criteria. Use perceptual tests or observable consequences to justify adopting conceptual models (e.g., fixed direction defined by absence of separation upon division).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue cross-disciplinary linking sciences for unification
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied Mathematics and Bio-physics are the two links between the three great divisions of science, and only when their work has been fully accomplished shall we be able to conceive all scientific formulae as laws of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage development of bridging disciplines that translate and apply abstract theoretical tools to concrete physical and biological problems; view integration across fields as essential for deeper unification of scientific laws.
